items.title: Bucky Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 23, 2003 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: George Barnes for instance, another great artist, single string player.

ctx.x: Oh definitely. I think the history of whatever you’re talking about has to be known by the student, before he understands what he’s about to do. Because he’s liable to come and say hey lookit I’m doing this. It’s been done before. And the other time they go in blindly and not know that you can do it with a lot of chords, you can do this and you can do that, you have to know what preceded you. And the guitar being the newest instrument of all the instruments, you’re not going that far back, I’d say 1933, ’32,…

pay a little attention and listen to what went on. Eddie Lang, Charlie Christian. It’s all different. Carl Kress. And there’s a lot of history there. And George Van Eps, I mean there’s some stuff that those guys did that will never be repeated. They did it off the cuff. And you have to understand that. Just to go in blindly and start playing the guitar is not going to help you. Because later on in life, you go 20 years from now, and they miss this whole thing. George Barnes for instance, another great artist,…
Yeah and a lot of people recently have said they think the students coming out of the music schools now sound sort of the same—

items.title: Ruth & Bucky Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, Saddle River, New Jersey, January 19, 2015
items.q: George Barnes as a soloist. If they didn’t need a soloist they wouldn’t hire them.

ctx.x: Sounds like some kind of project for somebody to do. Okay so this is sort of an obvious question. But why did you and Barry Galbraith and Milt Hinton, how come you were on the A team? Why was it that you got the calls?

I don’t know, because I thought maybe because I played rhythm guitar, and there was always room on a recording session to play rhythm. And that’s what I was known for. Al Caiola and Tony Mottola were known for soloists. George Barnes as a soloist. If they didn’t need a soloist they wouldn’t hire them. They just had rhythm guitar. That’s one thing they had to have on a record. Bomp-chink, bomp-chink. And that I knew I could do very well.
Did Freddie Green hip you to that?

items.title: Bucky Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: After the Tonight Show I’d go over there and play with George. And we got some good notices and we made an album, we made two albums.

ctx.x: When you got together to do a duo record with some of those people, mostly just talking through tunes, picking out tunes, did you rehearse it a lot?

Well at first I would say with Tony Mottola, Tony took advantage of the seven string and we made a couple of beautiful records together because Tony was a very lyrical player. And then the same with George Barnes, and it was a different approach. George and I went through a fake book one night out in Jersey with the machine, the recording machine on, we played one tune after another, like just turned page after page. Go into it, play it, and we had, oh we had enough for about ten albums. But it was the beginning…
